generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology research often collects sensitive personal data, so the duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity carry real weight. Participants agree to take part on the understanding that their responses are secure and that they cannot be identified in any write-up. Where a study involves children or clinical populations, these duties tighten, and the research ethics committee expects to see the extra safeguards.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students finish the same set of participant interviews on social anxiety and turn to writing up.

Tom quotes participants by name, emails the raw recordings to a collaborator without asking, and keeps the files on a personal laptop. The write-up reads vividly, but consent was never secured for sharing, and named quotations make individuals identifiable. The duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity have all been missed.

Amara secures signed consent before sharing anything, stores the recordings securely, and reports participants as Participant A and Participant B. Where a participant is under eighteen, she checks the extra requirements with the research ethics committee first. The data still tells its story, but no one can be identified from it.

Both students gathered the same material. Only Amara treated the people behind the data as owed confidentiality, consent and anonymity.
generatedProse.summary: Collecting data in psychology brings duties to the people who provide it. You can now apply the duties of confidentiality, consent and anonymity, justify the extra care that children and clinical participants require, and appraise how data should be secured, shared and anonymised. The final lesson widens the view to rigour across the whole project.

check.body: Why does psychology research involving children or clinical populations call for additional care?

items.text: Because they may be less able to give fully informed, voluntary consent, so extra safeguards and expert advice are needed.
Because their data is more interesting to examiners.
Because anonymisation is not required for children.
Because consent forms do not apply to anyone under eighteen.

feedback.correct: That's right. Reduced capacity to give informed, voluntary consent means extra safeguards and advice are needed.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Think about capacity to consent, not convenience.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Children and clinical participants may be less able to consent fully, so the duties tighten and expert advice is needed; they do not relax.
